summary: Specifies the media type for carrying PKCS #10 certification requests from RFC 2986. It carries over the specification from RFC 2311, which was moved to Historic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A label saying 'this is a request for a digital ID card'.

questions: what is a pkcs10 certification request
what file extension does pkcs10 use
how is a pkcs10 request encoded for email
subtitle: The media type label for sending a PKCS #10 certificate request, carried over from an old S/MIME RFC.

tldr.problem: The application/pkcs10 media type was defined in RFC 2311, which was moved to Historic, so the IANA registration pointed at a Historic document and the PKCS #10 specification did not describe the type.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5967 carries the definition over: the body MUST be a PKCS #10 CertificationRequest, preferably DER-encoded and base64-encoded for 7-bit transports, and it redoes the IANA registration.
tldr.outcome: The registration now points to a non-Historic document, and RFC 5967 formally updates RFC 2986.

today: RFC 5967 is an Informational RFC that updates RFC 2986. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why This Document Exists
sections.content:
RFC 2311 first defined the application/pkcs10 media type. When RFC 2633 was published, that section was dropped, but the text was not added to the PKCS #10 document, RFC 2986. Later, RFC 5751 moved RFC 2311 to Historic status.

To make sure the IANA media type registration points at a non-Historic document, RFC 5967 updates RFC 2986 with the definition of the type and a new IANA registration based on RFC 4288. The text of its Section 2 is adapted from Section 3.7 of RFC 2311.
sections.eli5: An old rulebook that described the label got retired, and the new rulebook forgot to copy it. This document puts the label description back where it belongs.

sections.title: The Body Format
sections.content:
PKCS #10 defines the ASN.1 type CertificationRequest, used to ask a Certification Authority (CA) for a certificate. When the media type application/pkcs10 is used, the body MUST be a CertificationRequest.

A robust application SHOULD output Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER) but accept Basic Encoding Rules (BER) or DER on input. BER and DER produce 8-bit data, so where a transport is limited to 7-bit data a suitable 7-bit transfer encoding MUST be applied. In MIME-compatible transports, base64 SHOULD be used.
sections.eli5: The envelope must hold a properly filled-in request form. Write it in the tidy, standard way, and if the post office only handles plain letters, turn it into plain letters first.

sections.title: Sending a Request
sections.content:
To send a certificate-signing request, the application/pkcs10 message format MUST be used. Certificates and CRLs without signed content are different: they use application/pkcs7-mime instead.

The sender places the cryptographic information in a CertificationRequest, encodes it as BER or DER (DER preferred), and typically base64-encodes it so it is 7-bit data suitable for ESMTP. The result becomes the body of an application/pkcs10 body part. Recovering and processing the request on the CA side is left out of scope.
sections.eli5: You fill in the form, fold it the standard way, turn it into plain letters, and put it in an envelope marked with the right label.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
IANA updated the registration of the pkcs10 subtype in the Application Media Types registry, using the template from BCP 13. The type name is application, there are no required or optional parameters, and the encoding is binary.

The registration lists .p10 as the file extension, no magic number, an intended usage of COMMON, and the IESG as change controller.
sections.eli5: The official list of envelope labels now has this label filled in properly, with the file ending .p10.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 2986 and RFC 5751 apply. RFC 5967 introduces no new ones. The registration notes that clients use a certification request to ask a CA to certify a public key, and that the request is digitally signed.
sections.eli5: Nothing new to worry about: the request is signed, and the older rules still apply.

data.title: An application/pkcs10 body part
data.code:
Content-Type: application/pkcs10; name=smime.p10
Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64
Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=smime.p10
